title: Neural Orbit
subtitle: Build the constellation in your head, one concept at a time.

levels.name: Explorer
levels.subtitle: Read the basic state of the constellation
levels.summary: You can now read the basic state of the constellation: almost everything is near 465.5 km, one orbit takes about 93.9 minutes, and the population resolves into 11 shells across 5 inclination families.

levels.name: Analyst
levels.subtitle: See the structure behind the points
levels.summary: You can now see structure: RAAN sets a plane's orientation, J2 predicts its drift to within 0.066% at the median, and migration is shell-specific rather than one global lowering.

levels.name: Operator
levels.subtitle: Connect geometry to service
levels.summary: You can now connect geometry to service: a 25 degree mask leaves a median of 55 visible satellites, the best-satellite handover is about 30 seconds, and Doppler reaches 233.6 kHz at p95.

levels.name: Researcher
levels.subtitle: Audit the evidence, not just the result
levels.summary: You can now audit the evidence: SGP4 is validated against 640 official vectors, the 45-claim ledger separates verified from external-only statements, and 6.19-6.27 ms is radio-only latency, not an end-to-end promise.

concepts.label: Low Earth orbit
concepts.definition: Low Earth orbit is the region below about 2,000 km. The median Starlink object in the 2026-11-23 snapshot is at 465.5 km.
concepts.why: Low altitude reduces the radio path, but it also means faster orbital motion and frequent handovers.

concepts.label: Orbital period
concepts.definition: The median orbit takes 93.9 minutes, or about 15.3 orbits per day.
concepts.why: The period sets how quickly the geometry changes and how often a site must switch satellites.

concepts.label: Altitude shell
concepts.short: A cluster, not a single ring
concepts.definition: A shell is a cluster of similar altitude and inclination. The atlas resolves 11 shells across 5 inclination families.
concepts.why: A single average altitude hides the structure that matters for coverage and migration.

concepts.label: Inclination
concepts.definition: Inclination is the angle between the orbital plane and the equator. It controls the maximum latitude the orbit can reach.
concepts.why: The family mix explains why coverage is not uniform across the planet.

concepts.label: Public snapshot
concepts.definition: A snapshot is a time-stamped public catalog. It is not a live telemetry feed and not a census of everything ever launched.
concepts.why: Every comparison in the atlas starts with a frozen snapshot, so the result can be checked.

concepts.label: RAAN
concepts.definition: RAAN is the right ascension of the ascending node: where the orbital plane crosses the equator going north.
concepts.why: Two satellites at the same altitude can be in different planes. RAAN tells them apart.

concepts.label: Orbital plane
concepts.short: A family of orbits with the same orientation
concepts.definition: An effective plane is a cluster of similar RAAN after J2 rectification. The four largest shells show 92, 124, 23, and 62 effective groups.
concepts.why: Plane structure affects how the constellation spreads coverage around the planet.

concepts.label: J2 nodal regression
concepts.definition: Earth is not a perfect sphere. Its equatorial bulge causes RAAN to drift. The median J2 prediction error in the atlas is 0.066%.
concepts.why: Without removing J2 drift, plane comparisons mix real structure with a predictable clock.

concepts.label: Shell migration
concepts.definition: Migration is the change in a shell's altitude over time. It is shell-specific: the 43 degree shell is stable, while the 70 degree shell moved by about -97 km.
concepts.why: A global average can hide a large change in one shell and a stable population in another.

concepts.label: Effective plane count
concepts.definition: The plane counts are effective RAAN clusters, not official Walker design numbers. Merged or partially filled planes change the measured lattice.
concepts.why: Calling an effective count a design number would overstate what public data can prove.

concepts.label: Coverage geometry
concepts.definition: A 10-site, 24-hour geometric simulation with a 25 degree elevation mask finds a median of 55.0 visible satellites per site, with a range of 21-65.
concepts.why: Coverage is abundant in this geometric model, but abundance is not the same as operational service quality.

concepts.label: Handover
concepts.definition: A handover is a change in the serving satellite. In the best-satellite model the median interval is 30.0 seconds.
concepts.why: Frequent handovers are a consequence of low altitude and fast orbital motion.

concepts.label: Doppler shift
concepts.definition: Doppler shift is the change in observed frequency caused by relative motion. The median p95 pass maximum is 233.6 kHz in this model.
concepts.why: Doppler is a measurable signature of the pass geometry and a practical radio design constraint.

concepts.label: Decay and attrition
concepts.short: Missing is not the same as reentered
concepts.definition: A satellite missing from a later catalog is catalog attrition, not confirmed reentry. The SATCAT extract contains only on-orbit objects.
concepts.why: The distinction keeps a data gap from becoming an unsupported physical claim.

concepts.label: Orbit-control maneuver
concepts.short: A discrete step in the elements
concepts.definition: The TLE panel shows 510 discrete orbit-control steps across 15 satellites: 448 raises and 62 lowers.
concepts.why: Maneuvers are observable in public mean elements, but they are not a complete operator manifest.

concepts.label: SGP4 propagation
concepts.definition: SGP4 turns mean orbital elements into positions and velocities. The implementation is checked against 640 official vectors with a maximum position difference of 1.171e-07 km.
concepts.why: A validated propagator is the difference between a plausible picture and a reproducible measurement.

concepts.label: Claim ledger
concepts.definition: The ledger contains 45 claims: 20 verified, 7 consistent, 5 partially verified, and 13 external-only. Each claim points to evidence or an explicit outside source.
concepts.why: A professional result states not only what is known, but also how strongly it is known.

concepts.label: Radio-path latency
concepts.definition: The radio-only four-leg RTT bounds are 6.19-6.27 ms. This is not an end-to-end internet latency measurement.
concepts.why: The distinction prevents a geometric bound from being sold as a user-observed service guarantee.

concepts.label: Gateway assumption
concepts.definition: Public orbital data does not include gateway coordinates. The model therefore reports bounds: one with the gateway at nadir and one colocated with the user.
concepts.why: Naming the missing input is more honest than inventing a route.

concepts.label: External-only evidence
concepts.definition: External-only means a statement is not tested in this study and relies on an operator, public report, or cited paper. It is not a hidden measurement.
concepts.why: A clear boundary between measured and reported claims makes the atlas usable in due diligence.

questions.prompt: What is the median altitude of the 2026-11-23 Starlink snapshot?
questions.explain: The measured median is 465.5 km. The old 550 km shorthand describes the historical upper shell, not the 2026 median.

questions.prompt: About how long does one Starlink orbit take?
questions.explain: The median orbital period is 93.9 minutes, or about 15.3 orbits per day.

questions.prompt: What is a shell in this atlas?
options: A cluster of similar altitude and inclination
questions.explain: A shell is a resolved cluster, not a single ring. The atlas finds 11 shells across 5 inclination families.

questions.prompt: What does inclination control?
options: The maximum latitude the orbit can reach
questions.explain: Inclination is the angle between the orbital plane and the equator. It limits how far north and south the satellite can travel.

questions.prompt: What is a public snapshot?
options: A time-stamped public catalog, not a live feed
questions.explain: A snapshot is frozen and time-stamped. That is what makes the comparison reproducible.

questions.prompt: What does RAAN describe?
options: The orientation of the orbital plane around Earth's axis
questions.explain: RAAN locates where the plane crosses the equator going north. Two satellites at the same altitude can have different RAAN values.

questions.prompt: How does this atlas count planes?
options: As effective RAAN clusters after J2 rectification
questions.explain: The counts are effective clusters. Merged or partially filled planes make them different from a clean design number.

questions.prompt: What does J2 nodal regression explain?
options: Steady RAAN drift caused by Earth's equatorial bulge
questions.explain: Earth's bulge makes the orbital plane precess. The measured median disagreement with the J2 prediction is 0.066%.

questions.prompt: Which shell was essentially stable between April and November 2026?
questions.explain: The 43 degree shell is the quiet one. The 70 degree shell moved by about -97 km, and the 97.4 degree shell also descended.

questions.prompt: Why are the plane counts not design Walker numbers?
options: All satellites are in one plane
Merged or partially filled planes change the effective lattice
questions.explain: The atlas measures the lattice that the public data actually shows. It does not claim to know the operator's design intent.

questions.prompt: With a 25 degree elevation mask, what is the median number of visible satellites per site?
questions.explain: The median is 55 visible satellites, with a per-site range of 21-65.

questions.prompt: What is a handover?
questions.explain: A handover is a change in the serving satellite. The median best-satellite interval is 30.0 seconds.

questions.prompt: What causes Doppler shift in this model?
options: Relative motion between satellite and ground site
questions.explain: Relative motion changes the observed frequency. The median p95 pass maximum is 233.6 kHz.

questions.prompt: A satellite missing from a later catalog means what?
questions.explain: The SATCAT extract contains only on-orbit objects. A missing name is a catalog signal, not proof of reentry.

questions.prompt: What is a maneuver event in the TLE panel?
questions.explain: The panel contains 510 discrete steps across 15 satellites. It is a measurable signature, not a complete operator manifest.

questions.prompt: What is SGP4 used for?
options: Propagating mean elements to positions and velocities
questions.explain: SGP4 is the standard propagator. The atlas validates it against 640 official vectors.

questions.prompt: What does the claim ledger do?
options: Maps each claim to evidence and an explicit status
questions.explain: The ledger separates verified, consistent, partially verified, and external-only statements. That is how a reader sees the strength of each claim.

questions.prompt: What do the 6.19-6.27 ms numbers describe?
options: A radio-only four-leg path bound, not end-to-end latency
questions.explain: The model excludes fiber, processing, scheduling, weather, and load. It is a geometric radio bound, not a user-observed promise.

questions.prompt: Why is latency reported as bounds?
options: Public data does not include gateway coordinates
questions.explain: Without gateway coordinates, the atlas places the gateway at two transparent extremes and reports the range.

questions.prompt: What does external_only mean?
options: Not tested here; relies on an outside source
questions.explain: External-only is an honest label. It tells the reader that the statement is outside this study's measurement boundary.

final: The atlas is a chain: public snapshot, mean elements, shells and planes, dynamics, service geometry, and a claim ledger. Each link is reproducible, and each limit is stated. That is the professional standard. You now know more than most interview candidates.
